questions.q: How does an indexer's hosting problem differ from a dApp frontend's?
options: An indexer never needs to run continuously, only on a fixed daily schedule
An indexer is a long-running process that must stay continuously up, not a mostly-static build served once from a CDN
A frontend requires more uptime guarantees than an indexer
There is no difference -- both should be hosted exactly the same way
questions.explain: A frontend is built once and served statically; an indexer watches the chain continuously and must stay running, which is a different operational problem.

questions.q: What does a container platform's dashboard make visible that a static frontend deploy doesn't?
options: Whether a pull request's tests passed
The Solidity source code of the contracts the service reads from
The gas cost of the service's on-chain transactions
Whether a long-running process is actually still up, or silently crash-looping, in real time
questions.explain: A container dashboard shows what's actually running right now -- a crash-looping container shows up as restarting, unlike a static build that either deployed or failed to.

questions.q: Why pull a specific, pinned, published base image instead of hand-building one or floating on a tag like 'latest'?
options: Floating tags like 'latest' are required by Docker and cannot be avoided
Pinned images cannot contain any vulnerabilities
The same reproducibility argument as pinning a Solidity compiler version -- an unpinned base image means the build isn't reproducible
Pinning a base image version removes the need to ever scan it
questions.explain: A pinned, published image is reproducible the same way a pinned compiler version is -- 'it worked on my machine' becomes a checkable fact, not a guess.

questions.q: What does scanning a container image for known vulnerabilities before it ships accomplish?
options: It replaces the need for a Dockerfile entirely
It only matters for images that will never be deployed to production
It's the container-world equivalent of running Slither in CI -- an automated check catching a known class of problem before a human has to notice it
It guarantees the application code itself has no bugs
questions.explain: Image scanning automatically flags known CVEs in a base image's dependencies, the same role Slither plays for smart contract code in Chapter 2, Lesson 10.

questions.q: In the example Dockerfile, what does running as a non-root 'node' user accomplish?
options: It is required for npm ci to function at all
It automatically patches any vulnerabilities in the base image
It makes the container start faster
It limits what a compromised process inside the container can do, compared to running as root
questions.explain: Running as an unprivileged user is a containment measure -- if the process is compromised, it doesn't automatically have root-level access inside the container.
